title: Two Hostesses, Two Invitations
overview: Wisdom and Folly are pictured as two women calling from the city's high places, each inviting inexperienced people to a very different meal with a very different outcome.

parts.label: Wisdom prepares a feast (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Wisdom is a generous hostess who builds a fine house, cooks meat, mixes spiced wine and sends her servants out with invitations. The seven pillars probably suggest a complete, solid house, though scholars are unsure of the exact meaning.

parts.label: Her open invitation (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: She invites not the clever but the "simple," meaning inexperienced people who are easily led, and offers them both a meal and a new way to live. Christians have often read this feast alongside Jesus' stories of a great banquet open to everyone.

parts.label: Who can be taught (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: A mocker answers correction with insults, while a wise person welcomes it and grows wiser still. The point seems to be that openness to correction is what makes learning possible.

parts.label: Where wisdom begins (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: Here the "fear of the LORD" means deep respect and awe toward God, and real wisdom is said to start there and lead to a longer life. Each person carries the results of their own choices, wise or mocking.

parts.label: Folly copies the call (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: Folly is a loud, empty woman who sits high in the city like Wisdom and repeats Wisdom's exact invitation. She targets the same easily led people, even those simply going about their business.

parts.label: The pull of forbidden things (vv. 17-18)
parts.note: She claims that water taken by theft and food eaten in secret taste better, a saying many read as hinting at sexual unfaithfulness. But her guests end up deep in the grave, the place of the dead, meaning her path leads to ruin.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Wisdom pictured as a woman here is a poetic way of describing God's wisdom or a foreshadowing of Christ himself, as many older readers held.
think: When something feels sweeter precisely because it is forbidden or hidden, what do you think makes it feel that way?
